entries.dog|Fading Puppy Syndrome:
[Initial management within 1 hour of discovery determines survival]

(1) Temperature measurement and rewarming: measure rectal temperature (<35°C = hypothermia, <34°C = severe). Rapid rewarming is contraindicated because it causes shock through peripheral vasodilation. Gradual rewarming: use warm towels, a heat lamp (kept 45-50 cm away), or an incubator to raise temperature to 35-36°C over 30-60 minutes, then target 37-38°C. Never feed milk to a hypothermic puppy (the gut is not motile, leading to gastric fermentation → abdominal distension and death).

(2) Correction of hypoglycemia (only after body temperature is ≥35°C): give 5-10% dextrose solution 0.5-1.0 mL/100 g body weight orally (small amounts sublingually) or subcutaneously (SC). If no improvement, establish venous access (lateral saphenous vein or intraosseous route) and maintain with 2.5-5% dextrose in lactated Ringer's solution. Target BG >70 mg/dL.

(3) Dehydration and electrolytes: subcutaneous fluids (warmed lactated Ringer's 30-40 mL/kg/day in divided doses, SC) or oral rehydration (neonatal ORS). For severe dehydration, establish venous access and give LRS 10-15 mL/kg/hr.

(4) Exclusion and treatment of infection: umbilical disinfection (at birth: 10% povidone-iodine dip). For suspected sepsis, broad-spectrum antimicrobials — amoxicillin 15-20 mg/kg PO/SC q12h (enteric bacterial coverage) or ampicillin 20-30 mg/kg SC q8h. Do not use fluoroquinolones in neonates because of articular cartilage toxicity. Suspected CHV-1 (sudden death of multiple littermates, vulvar vesicles in the dam): maintain ambient temperature at 32-35°C (viral replication is suppressed at ≥38°C). Acyclovir (5 mg/kg SC q8h) is sometimes attempted, but evidence is limited.

(5) Nursing and nutrition: attempt nursing after rewarming and correction of hypoglycemia. If the suckling reflex is weak, tube-feed via catheter (French 5-8) — dam's milk or canine milk replacer (pet milk) at 0.13-0.2 mL per 1 g body weight every 2-3 hours. Caution: overfeeding (>5 mL/100 g/feeding) causes aspiration and abdominal distension.

(6) Check for congenital anomalies: palpate the palate (cleft palate), confirm a patent anus (atresia ani), auscultate for heart murmurs (congenital heart disease). For severe congenital anomalies not amenable to surgical correction, include euthanasia among the options.

(7) Body weight monitoring: record birth weight and weigh daily at the same time. A 10% increase over birth weight within the first 24 hours is essential. No weight gain for 12-24 hours = indication for urgent intervention. During the first week of life, aim for a daily gain of 5-10% (Mila et al. 2015).
entries.dog|Neonatal Puppy Mortality / Perinatal:
[Time-course management]

(1) Resuscitation immediately after delivery (0-2 hours):
- Airway clearance (suction nose/oropharynx with a bulb syringe; swinging is contraindicated — risk of intracranial hemorrhage)
- Vigorous stimulation with a towel (30-60 seconds) → confirm return of skin pinkness, vocalization and spontaneous breathing
- Respiratory arrest: oxygen by mask/tube, chest compressions 100-120/min, doxapram 1 drop (0.1-0.5 mg) sublingually (with caution; beware of induced tachycardia), epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg intratracheally or IV via the umbilical vein
- Rewarming: warm gradually to 35-37°C
- Naloxone: if opioids were used in the dam → 0.01-0.04 mg/kg SC/sublingually to the pup (reverses respiratory depression)

(2) Weighing and recording (at birth and daily):
Record the birth weight of every pup. Identify LBW/VLBW pups and monitor them preferentially. Pups falling below the weight-gain standard (5-10% daily gain in the first week of life) should receive supplemental feeding immediately.

(3) Colostrum management (most critical within 1-2 hours after birth):
Confirm colostrum intake (observe suckling behavior and contact with the teats). If lactation is inadequate or the pup is weak, give expressed colostrum or bovine colostrum (0.5-1.0 mL/100g PO). After 24 hours of life, efficiency of passive immune transfer drops sharply due to reduced intestinal permeability.

(4) Management of hypothermia and hypoglycemia: follow the treatment for fading puppy syndrome (check temperature → rewarm → correct hypoglycemia → feed, in that order).

(5) Umbilical care: disinfect promptly after birth with 10% povidone-iodine and allow to dry. Treat omphalitis (redness, pus, swelling) with a broad-spectrum antimicrobial (amoxicillin 15-20 mg/kg SC q12h).

(6) Management of infection: if CHV-1 is suspected (sudden death of multiple pups in a litter), keep ambient temperature at 32-35°C (suppresses viral replication). Chlorine-based disinfectants (0.5% hypochlorite) are effective. For enteritis (diarrhea, weight loss), identify the cause by smear, PCR and fecal examination; symptomatic treatment (fluids, gut support) + cause-specific treatment.

(7) Necropsy of dead pups: when multiple deaths occur within a litter, necropsy (post-mortem examination) is recommended — identifying the cause improves management of surviving pups and prevention in the next litter. Ship the body refrigerated (not frozen) to a veterinary pathology laboratory.
entries.fish|Aeromonas / Motile Aeromonad Septic: Antimicrobial bath (oxolinic acid, enrofloxacin), medicated feed, water-quality improvement. Severe cases with dropsy (pinecone scales) or ascites are difficult to treat.
entries.fish|Ammonia Poisoning: Immediate large water change (50-75%). Use bacterial additives, reduce feeding, use an ammonia remover.
entries.fish|Anchor Worm (Lernaea): Remove adult parasites with forceps, then disinfect the wound. Trichlorfon (Dipterex) bath, levamisole bath. Larval stages must also be controlled.
entries.fish|Columnaris Disease: Antimicrobial bath (oxolinic acid, kanamycin), salt bath, water-quality improvement. Medicated feed in severe cases.
entries.fish|Costia (Ichthyobodo): Formalin bath, salt bath, malachite green bath, raised water temperature.
entries.fish|Dropsy (Pinecone Disease): Epsom salt bath (magnesium sulfate), antimicrobial bath / medicated feed, water-quality improvement. Prognosis is generally poor.
entries.fish|Egg Binding (Dystocia): Raise water temperature, Epsom salt bath, provide spawning substrate. In severe cases, manual stripping of eggs under anesthesia.
entries.fish|Fish Lice (Argulus): Trichlorfon bath, removal with forceps, salt bath. In ponds, a complete water change is also effective.
entries.fish|Gill Flukes (Dactylogyrus): Praziquantel bath, formalin bath, trichlorfon bath. Combine with antimicrobials in severe cases.
entries.fish|Hexamita / Spironucleus (Internal F: Metronidazole medicated feed or bath, raised water temperature, nutritional improvement.
entries.fish|Hole-in-the-Head Disease (HITH / HL: Metronidazole bath or medicated feed, nutritional improvement (vitamin/mineral supplementation), water-quality improvement, removal of activated carbon.
entries.fish|Ichthyophthirius (White Spot Diseas: Raise water temperature to 28-30°C to accelerate the life cycle. 0.3-0.5% salt bath, methylene blue, malachite green, formalin bath. Drugs are effective only against the free-swimming (theront) stage.
entries.fish|Koi Herpesvirus Disease (KHV / CyHV: No specific treatment. Isolate the affected water body and restrict movement of fish. Raising water temperature to ≥30°C may reduce signs (risk of creating carriers).
entries.fish|Lymphocystis: No specific treatment; lesions regress spontaneously. Manage water quality to prevent secondary infection. Surgical removal in severe cases.
entries.fish|Marine Ich (Cryptocaryon irritans): Copper-ion preparations (in a hospital tank), hyposalinity (specific gravity 1.009), formalin bath. Copper must not be used in coral/invertebrate tanks.
entries.fish|Mycobacteriosis (Fish Tuberculosis): No effective treatment. Isolation and culling of infected fish is recommended. Thoroughly disinfect tanks and equipment. Avoid handling with bare hands (zoonotic).
entries.fish|Neon Tetra Disease (Pleistophora): No effective treatment. Isolate and cull infected fish. Disinfect tanks and equipment.
entries.fish|Nitrite Poisoning (Brown Blood Dise: Large water change, add salt (0.1-0.3% — chloride ions inhibit nitrite uptake), increase aeration.
entries.fish|Saprolegnia (Water Mold / Cotton Wo: Methylene blue bath, malachite green bath, salt bath (0.3-0.5%). Remove the underlying cause (treat wounds, improve water quality).
entries.fish|Skin Flukes (Gyrodactylus): Praziquantel bath, formalin bath, salt bath.
entries.fish|Spring Viremia of Carp (SVC): No specific treatment. Supportive care, prevention of secondary infection, stress reduction. Notifiable disease.
entries.fish|Swim Bladder Disorder: Fast for 3 days, then feed boiled, shelled food (e.g. green peas). Keep water temperature within the appropriate range. Antimicrobials if bacterial infection is suspected.
entries.fish|Trichodina: Formalin bath, salt bath, water-quality improvement. Correcting the underlying cause is essential.
entries.fish|Velvet Disease (Oodinium / Piscinoo: Copper-ion preparations (marine), methylene blue / acriflavine (freshwater), darkening the tank (inhibits photosynthesis), raised water temperature.
entries.fish|pH Shock: Gradual water-chemistry adjustment. Identify and remove the cause of the sudden change. Severe shock may be irreversible.
entries.horse|Acorn / Oak Toxicosis (Tannin Pois: Remove the cause: block access to acorns/oak. Fluid therapy: high-volume IV lactated Ringer's solution (maintain renal perfusion — initially 5-10 L/hr).  Diuresis: furosemide 1 mg/kg IV (if oliguric — after renal perfusion is secured). GI protection: mineral oil 2-4 L PO (to evacuate residual toxin).  Activated charcoal 1-3 g/kg PO (early after ingestion). Hypoproteinemia: plasma transfusion 6-10 L IV. NSAIDs are contraindicated (worsen nephrotoxicity). Pain management: butorphanol 0.01-0.05 mg/kg IV (not nephrotoxic). Electrolyte correction: KCl, NaHCO₃ (if metabolic acidosis). Prevention: fencing during the autumn acorn-drop season, adequate forage supply. Prognosis: can improve with early detection and fluid therapy. Poor prognosis in cases progressing to acute renal failure.
entries.horse|Acorn Toxicity: [Acorn toxicity (tannin toxicity) in horses] Blocking access to acorns/oak leaves is the top priority. Activated charcoal 1-2 g/kg PO (via nasogastric tube). Aggressive fluid therapy (lactated Ringer's IV, maintain renal perfusion → renal tubular necrosis is the main lesion). NSAIDs contraindicated (due to worsening nephrotoxicity). Frequent monitoring of BUN/Cre and electrolytes (every 12-24 hours). Oral calcium hydroxide (tannin neutralization). Prognosis depends on the degree of renal injury. Occurs predominantly in autumn.
entries.horse|Acute Renal Failure: [Equine Acute Renal Failure] High-volume fluid therapy: lactated Ringer's solution 4-8 L/hr IV initially. Immediate discontinuation of nephrotoxic drugs (gentamicin, NSAIDs, tetracycline). Promote diuresis: furosemide 1 mg/kg IV. Dopamine 3-5 μg/kg/min CRI (increase renal blood flow). Electrolyte correction (especially K, Ca). Search for the cause (nephrotoxic, haemodynamic, obstructive). BUN/Cre monitoring. Prognosis depends on the presence and duration of oliguria.
entries.horse|Aflatoxicosis: [Aflatoxicosis] Immediate removal of contaminated feed. Hepatoprotection: SAMe 20 mg/kg PO q24h, silymarin 4 mg/kg PO q24h. Fluid therapy (containing 5% dextrose). Vitamin K1 0.5-1 mg/kg IM q12h (if coagulopathy). Activated charcoal 1-2 g/kg PO (acute ingestion). Low-protein diet. Prognosis depends on the degree of hepatic damage. Test feed for aflatoxin (harmful at >20ppb).
entries.horse|Aminoglycoside Nephrotoxicity: Discontinue the aminoglycoside. Change to an alternative antimicrobial. Fluid therapy: high-volume IV lactated Ringer's solution (maintain renal perfusion, promote toxin excretion).  Diuresis: furosemide 1 mg/kg IV (if oliguric — only after adequate fluid volume is ensured).  Mannitol 0.25-0.5 g/kg IV (osmotic diuresis — to prevent progression to oliguria). Electrolyte correction: KCl, NaHCO₃. Avoid NSAIDs (further reduce renal blood flow). For pain: butorphanol. Nutritional management: low-protein feed, good-quality hay. Prevention: use once-daily dosing of gentamicin (6.6 mg/kg IV q24h) —   ensuring adequate peak levels + lower trough levels reduces the risk of nephrotoxicity.  Check hydration status before administration; monitor BUN/Cre regularly (every 3-5 days).  Avoid administration to dehydrated horses. Use particular caution in neonatal foals. Prognosis: recovery is possible with early detection and discontinuation. Progression to chronic renal failure carries a poor prognosis.
entries.horse|Anestrus / Ovarian Inactivity: [Diagnostic confirmation (mandatory before treatment)] (1) Transrectal ultrasound to assess ovarian morphology, follicle diameter, presence of CL and uterine tone. (2) Serum progesterone: >4 ng/mL → persistent CL (go to PGF2α); <1 ng/mL → true anestrus. (3) AMH: <0.05 ng/mL → senile failure or 63,XO (go to karyotyping); >2.5 ng/mL → suspect GCT. (4) Inhibin B: >0.7 ng/mL → GCT. (5) FSH/LH: elevated FSH + low LH → senile; both low → hypothalamic suppression. (6) Primary anestrus with small ovaries at >2 years of age → chromosomal testing (karyotyping, lymphocyte culture). (7) Endometrial biopsy (Kenney classification) grade III/IV → explain poor fertility prognosis. [Dosing basis] *In this section, converted values for a 500 kg mare are given alongside. Adjust actual doses individually for body weight, BCS and concurrent disease. [Seasonal anestrus] (a) Artificial photoperiod: start 12/1 - 1/15 (Northern Hemisphere; month/day); natural + artificial light totalling 16 hours/day (16h light / 8h dark, typically lights on 6:00-22:00), visual-level lux ≥100 (measured at the horse's eye level in the center of the stall). Light source: full-spectrum fluorescent lamps (4-8 W/m²) or one 100W incandescent bulb (one bulb per 10-12m² stall, on the ceiling at the center of the stall). Evidence update: 468 nm blue light (blue light mask, e.g. Equilume) for 3.5 hours/day (evening 16:30-20:00), worn over one eye, has equivalent efficacy (Murphy AAEP 2010, Equine Vet J 2014; light stimulus concentrated during the scotosensitive phase from evening dusk into night). Aim for the first ovulatory estrus 60-70 days later and the first ovulation in mid-January to early February. (b) Dopamine antagonist: domperidone Equidone gel 11% (110 mg/mL), dose 1.1 mg/kg PO SID × 10-21 days = 550 mg/day (5 mL gel) for a 500kg horse; efficacy increased in combination with long days (Besognet & Daels Theriogenology 1996). Alternatives: sulpiride injection 1 mg/kg IM BID (500 mg/dose for a 500kg horse, × 14-21 days), metoclopramide 0.2 mg/kg IM q8h (200kg - 1g/day). Beware of extrapyramidal signs with heavy, prolonged use. (c) Continuous GnRH administration: buserelin (Receptal 0.004 mg/mL) 40 μg IM q12h × 7-14 days = 10 mL/dose for a 500kg horse; for final ovulation trigger use deslorelin 1.5 mg IM single dose. GnRH pulsatile pump (research facilities): 250 ng/pulse SC q1h × 14 days (automated pump fitted). (d) Progestin priming: altrenogest Regu-Mate 0.22% (2.2 mg/mL) or Altresyn 4 mg/mL, dose 0.044 mg/kg PO SID × 10-15 days = 22 mg/day for a 500kg horse (Regu-Mate 10 mL / Altresyn 5.5 mL, top-dressed on feed). Combine with PGF2α (cloprostenol 250 μg IM) 24 hours after discontinuation → estrus and ovulation 7-10 days after discontinuation (efficacy increased with concurrent light therapy). Skin contact causes hormonal effects in humans (contraindicated for pregnant women, children and men alike) → gloves mandatory. [Prolonged spring transition] (a) Altrenogest 0.044 mg/kg PO SID × 10-14 days → cloprostenol 250 μg IM 24 hours after discontinuation; when follicle diameter reaches >35mm, induce ovulation with deslorelin 1.5 mg IM or hCG (Chorulon 1500 IU/vial) 2,500-3,000 IU IV (ovulation within 24-48 hours). (b) Concurrent domperidone 1.1 mg/kg PO SID increases response rate. (c) Alternative ovulation trigger: GnRH agonist Ovuplant 2.1 mg implant (subcutaneous; removal after 48 hours restores pituitary sensitivity, reusable). [Persistent corpus luteum (pseudoanestrus)] (a) Cloprostenol (Estrumate 250 μg/mL) 250 μg IM single dose = 1 mL / 500kg horse; ovulation 7-10 days later; if no ovulation, repeat after 14 days. (b) Dinoprost tromethamine (Lutalyse 5 mg/mL) 5-10 mg IM single dose = 1-2 mL for a 500kg horse (more side effects [sweating, colic-like signs] than cloprostenol). In cases with concurrent endometritis, perform uterine lavage + systemic antimicrobials first (see EED section below). Transient sweating and increased heart rate 30-60 minutes after administration, usually resolving within 2 hours. Pregnancy check mandatory (abortion if given during pregnancy). [Silent ovulation (silent heat)] Identify the ovulatory period (US: >35mm follicle, marked uterine edema) → trigger ovulation with deslorelin 1.5 mg IM or hCG 2,500-3,000 IU IV (ovulation 24-48 hours later); perform AI/breeding directly even without stallion response. To elicit behavioral estrus, estradiol benzoate 5-10 mg IM single dose (24 hours before breeding) or estradiol cypionate (ECP) 3-5 mg IM is sometimes used (improves teaser response). Increased teaser exposure (10-15 minutes daily) aids behavioral estrus detection. [Senile ovarian failure] Usually refractory to treatment. Abandon use as an embryo transfer donor; consider use as a recipient mare (artificial cycle synchronization with GnRH agonist deslorelin 1.5 mg IM + estradiol 17β 50 mg IM SID × 4 days). Oocyte aspiration + ICSI success rate <10%. [Granulosa cell tumor] Unilateral ovariectomy (standing laparoscopic or flank approach): contralateral ovarian function recovers 3-12 months post-operatively; 80% can become pregnant the next season (McCue & Roser JAVMA 2007). Post-operative antimicrobials: procaine penicillin 22,000 IU/kg IM q12h × 5 days + gentamicin 6.6 mg/kg IV SID × 5 days, flunixin 1.1 mg/kg IV q12h × 3 days. [Concurrent PPID] Pergolide mesylate (Prascend 1 mg tablet): start 2 μg/kg PO SID = 1 mg/day (1 tablet) for a 500kg horse; recheck ACTH after 4 weeks; if inadequate, titrate up to 4 μg/kg/day (2 mg, 2 tablets), maximum 8 μg/kg/day. For inappetence at induction (10-15%), start at half a tablet and increase to the full dose over 1-2 weeks. Estrous cycles resume after ACTH normalization (several months to 1 year). [Hypothyroidism (rare)] Levothyroxine sodium 0.022 mg/kg PO SID = 11 mg/day for a 500kg horse (approximately 1 scoop of Thyro-L 12 g/oz powder); recheck fT4 after 4-6 weeks. [Nutritional] Gradually adjust to BCS 5-6/9 (0.5-1 point per week). Thin (BCS<4): concentrate 1-2% of body weight/day, vegetable oil 0.5-1 mL/kg PO SID (corn, soybean, rice bran oil), protein 12-14% CP, lysine 0.7% or more. Obese (BCS>8): feed restriction (hay 1.5-2.0% BW/day, mainly grass hay) + exercise. Supplements: Se 3 mg/day (oral; Bo-Se injection 5 mL IM = 5 mg Se + 68 IU Vit E q14 days also acceptable), Vit E (α-tocopherol) 2,000 IU/day (natural-source d-α recommended), Cu 100-150 mg/day (Cu chelate), Zn 300-400 mg/day (Cu:Zn=1:3-4), β-carotene 200-400 mg/day (Carophyll Red, starting 60 days before the season), folic acid 20-40 mg/day. [Prognostic follow-up] Repeat transrectal ultrasound 7-21 days after starting treatment: follicular development (>20mm → ovulatory period), uterine edema (grade 0-3, with 2-3 being preovulatory), confirmation of ovulation. Day 14 pregnancy US (14-16 days after breeding). [References] McKinnon AO et al. Equine Reproduction 2nd ed (Wiley-Blackwell 2011) Ch.198-203 / Daels PF, Hughes JP. Theriogenology 1993 / Nagy P et al. Anim Reprod Sci 2000 / Donadeu FX, Watson ED. Reprod Domest Anim 2007 / McCue PM, Roser JF. JAVMA 2007 / Allen WR, Wilsher S. Equine Vet J 2009 / Murphy BA et al. Equine Vet J 2014 (blue light mask) / Besognet B, Daels PF. Theriogenology 1996 / AAEP Reproduction Manual / Plumb's Veterinary Drug Handbook 9th ed.
entries.horse|Anticoagulant Rodenticide Toxicity: [Acute hemorrhage] Vitamin K1 0.5-1.0 mg/kg SC q12h × 3-5 days → PO q12h × 2-6 weeks (second-generation anticoagulants have long half-lives and require prolonged treatment). IV administration is contraindicated (risk of anaphylaxis). Transfusion: whole blood transfusion for severe anemia (PCV<15%). Fresh frozen plasma (coagulation factor replacement). Fluids: maintain circulating blood volume. Stall rest (to reduce bleeding risk). After confirming normalization of PT, stop vitamin K1 for 48 hours and recheck (if prolonged again → continue treatment). Prognosis: good with early treatment. Guarded prognosis with massive hemorrhage or body-cavity hemorrhage.
entries.horse|Arsenic Poisoning: [Arsenic poisoning in horses] Decontamination: activated charcoal 1-3 g/kg. Chelators: dimercaprol (BAL) 3 mg/kg IM q4h × 2 days → q12h × 7 days, or succimer (DMSA) 10 mg/kg PO q8h. Fluid therapy (renal protection). GI protection: sucralfate. Electrolyte correction. Caused by ingestion of herbicides or rodenticides. Chronic exposure causes peripheral neuropathy.
entries.horse|Atypical Myopathy (Sycamore Maple: [Dosing basis] *Based on a 500 kg horse. Emergency — the most severe disease with a case fatality rate of 70-90%. [Immediate response] (1) Immediate removal from pasture (stop exposure — prevent ingestion of residual HGA). (2) High-volume IV fluids: isotonic crystalloids (LRS or Plasmalyte) 4-6 L/hr × 24-48 hours → maintenance (forced diuresis to promote myoglobin excretion and prevent AKI). Minimum 60-90 L/d. (3) B vitamins (coenzyme replacement, support of β-oxidation): thiamine B1 5-10 mg/kg IV q12h (2.5-5 g/dose in a 500 kg horse = 100-200 mL of 25 mg/mL), riboflavin B2 25-50 mg IV q24h, L-carnitine 100 mg/kg IV q12h (50 g/dose) — limited evidence but standard supportive care. (4) Vitamin E 5,000-10,000 IU IM/PO q24h (antioxidant, α-tocopherol). (5) Vitamin C 20-40 mg/kg IV q12h (10-20 g/dose) — antioxidant support. (6) Glycine 0.5-1 g/kg IV/PO q12h (promotes conjugation and excretion of HGA, limited evidence). [Analgesia] (7) Flunixin 1.1 mg/kg IV q12h (11 mL/dose of 50 mg/mL) — but use with caution and at low dose (0.25-0.5 mg/kg) when AKI is present. Phenylbutazone only when renal function is normal. (8) Morphine 0.05-0.1 mg/kg IM/IV q4-6h or butorphanol 0.01-0.02 mg/kg IV q4h. [Management of hyperkalaemia] (9) Continuous ECG monitoring; with hyperkalaemia (K>6.0 mmol/L): 10% calcium gluconate 0.5-1 mL/kg slow IV (cardioprotection), dextrose 50% 1 mL/kg IV + regular insulin 0.1 IU/kg IV, sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mEq/kg IV slow. [Intensive support of the recumbent horse] (10) Thick bedding, repositioning q4h (prevention of decubital ulcers and compartment syndrome), head positioning (aspiration prevention), eye drops and oral moistening, urinary catheter. (11) Nutrition: small frequent feeds if able to swallow; if not, IV nutrition (5-10% dextrose). [Laminitis prevention] (12) Ice baths for 24-72 hours, cautious use of phenylbutazone. [References] Votion et al. Equine Vet J 2014; Westermann et al. J Vet Intern Med 2008; van Galen et al. Equine Vet J 2012; Boemer et al. Equine Vet J 2015.
entries.horse|Avocado Toxicosis: [Avocado toxicosis in horses] No specific antidote. Supportive care is the mainstay: fluid therapy (lactated Ringer's solution IV, maintain circulating blood volume). Continuous ECG monitoring (risk of arrhythmia and myocardial necrosis due to persin-induced cardiotoxicity). Heart failure management: furosemide 1 mg/kg IV q12h, digoxin (in severe cases). In lactating mares, mastitis/sterile mammary necrosis → warm compresses to the udder and milking management. GI decontamination: activated charcoal 1-2 g/kg PO (perform early after ingestion). Prognosis depends on the amount ingested and duration of exposure. Fruit, leaves, seeds and bark all contain persin and are toxic to horses.
entries.horse|Black Locust Toxicity: [Black locust (Robinia pseudoacacia) toxicity] Gastrointestinal decontamination: activated charcoal 1-2 g/kg PO, mineral oil 4-8 mL/kg. Fluids (lactated Ringer's IV, correction of dehydration). Antiemetic/GI protection: sucralfate 20 mg/kg PO q6h. Pain management: flunixin 1.1 mg/kg IV q12h. ECG monitoring (watch for arrhythmias). The bark and seeds are the toxic parts (robinin). Most recover with supportive care.
entries.horse|Black Walnut Toxicity: [Black walnut toxicosis] Laminitis prevention is the top priority. Immediate removal of exposure (remove walnut shavings bedding, wash the limbs). Cryotherapy (immerse the limbs in ice water for 48h). NSAID: phenylbutazone 4.4 mg/kg PO → 2.2 mg/kg q12h. Dexamethasone 0.1 mg/kg IV (anti-inflammatory). Fluids. If laminitis develops, deep bedding + hoof pads. Do not use black walnut wood in the housing environment.
entries.horse|Blister Beetle Toxicity: [Blister beetle toxicosis (cantharidin)] Emergency. GI decontamination: mineral oil 2-4 L via nasogastric tube. Aggressive fluid therapy: IV lactated Ringer's solution. Renal protection: maintain diuresis. Flunixin 1.1 mg/kg IV q12h. Sucralfate 20-40 mg/kg PO q6h (GI protection). Calcium correction (if hypocalcemic). ECG monitoring. Lethal dose: approximately 1 mg/kg. Caused by beetles contaminating hay. Mortality 30-50%.
entries.horse|Blue-Green Algae Toxicity: [Blue-green algae (cyanobacteria) toxicity] Emergency. Decontamination: activated charcoal 1-3 g/kg via nasogastric tube (within 2h of ingestion). Hepatotoxic form (microcystins): fluid therapy, hepatoprotection (SAMe, silymarin). Neurotoxic form (anatoxin-a): diazepam 0.05 mg/kg IV for seizures. Oxygen for respiratory failure. No specific antidote. Poor prognosis (especially the neurotoxic form). Isolate from the contaminated water source.
entries.horse|Bracken Fern Toxicity: [Bracken Fern Toxicity] Thiamine (vitamin B1) 5-10 mg/kg IV/IM q12h × 3-5 days (aim: to counteract thiaminase) → then switch to oral maintenance dosing. Bone marrow suppression form (chronic): supportive care, blood transfusion (in pancytopenia), infection prevention. Remove the causative bracken from the pasture. Prognosis: the acute thiamine-deficiency form improves rapidly with B1 administration. The chronic bone marrow suppression form has a poor prognosis (irreversible haematopoietic failure). Prevention: bracken management in pastures (weed control, fencing).
entries.horse|Castor Bean Toxicity: [Castor bean (Ricinus) toxicity] Emergency. Ricin is a protein synthesis-inhibiting toxin with no antidote. Decontamination: activated charcoal 1-3 g/kg PO, mineral oil via nasogastric tube. Aggressive fluid therapy (maintain circulating blood volume). GI protection: sucralfate 20 mg/kg PO q6-8h. Blood glucose monitoring (risk of hypoglycemia → glucose supplementation). DIC management: fresh frozen plasma. Frequent testing of hepatic and renal function. The lethal dose is low and body-weight dependent; prognosis poor. Intensive care management is essential.
entries.horse|Chronic Pyrrolizidine Alkaloid Tox: No specific antidote. Immediately remove PA-containing plants and change pasture. Hepatic encephalopathy: lactulose 0.1-0.2 mL/kg PO q8h, neomycin 15-20 mg/kg PO q8h. Fluids (maintain hepatic perfusion, correct hypoglycemia). Vitamin E/Se, B vitamins. Photosensitization management: avoid direct sunlight (stable confinement). Low-protein diet (reduce ammonia production). High-quality roughage. Prognosis: once clinical signs appear there is extensive (irreversible) hepatic fibrosis and the prognosis is poor. Mortality >90%.
entries.horse|Clover Toxicity: [Clover toxicosis (slobbers syndrome / photosensitization)] Removal of the causative forage / change of pasture is the top priority. Slaframine type (salivation): usually resolves spontaneously within a few days after clover removal. Estrogen-like type (red clover): reproductive disorders → recovery after change of pasture. Photosensitization type: avoid sunlight, stable management. Supportive care: fluids, nutritional management. Most cases recover quickly after removal of the cause, with a good prognosis.
entries.horse|Colitis-X (Peracute Idiopathic Col: [Diagnosis] Diagnosis of exclusion (Salmonella, C. difficile, PHF, and right dorsal colitis must all be excluded). Early tests: CBC (leukopenia → leukocytosis within hours), lactate >4, PCV >55, TP <4.5, metabolic acidosis, electrolyte abnormalities. [Ultra-aggressive resuscitation (the golden hours)] Hypertonic saline 7.2% 4 mL/kg IV rapid (initial resuscitation), immediately followed by LRS 20-30 mL/kg/hr IV maintenance (two large-bore catheters). Plasma 6-10 L IV (colloid + anti-endotoxin antibodies), hetastarch 10 mL/kg. [Anti-endotoxin measures (essential)] Polymyxin B 6000 U/kg IV q8h (with renal function monitoring), flunixin 0.25 mg/kg IV q6h (low-dose anti-endotoxic), pentoxifylline 8 mg/kg PO q8h (TNF-α suppression), DMSO 0.1 g/kg IV q12h. [Intestinal protection] Bio-Sponge (DTOSmectite) 1-2 lb PO q6h (toxin binding), activated charcoal 1-3 g/kg PO. [Empirical broad-spectrum antimicrobials] Penicillin 22,000 U/kg IV q6h + gentamicin 6.6 mg/kg IV q24h, metronidazole 25 mg/kg PO/IV q8h (if concurrent C. diff suspected). [Vasopressors] Norepinephrine 0.1-1 μg/kg/min CRI if mean arterial pressure <60 mmHg. [Laminitis prevention] Continuous ice-water immersion of both forelimbs >72 hours. [ICU] Vital signs every 30 minutes, ECG, CVP, urine output, lactate trend. Assess response by lactate decline. [Poor prognostic factors] PCV >65 at onset, lactate >8, K+ <2.5, refractory hypotension, urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hr. [Long-term management of survivors] Prolonged hypoproteinemia during convalescence, intestinal mucosal repair (prebiotics/probiotics such as CP Powder), monitoring of intestinal function for 6-12 months.
entries.horse|Colonic Fibrous Phytobezoar: [Diagnosis] Rectal examination palpates a hard foreign-body-like mass in the small colon/pelvic inlet; radiography (foals, small horses) or ultrasonography confirms a hyperechoic foreign body within the colon; peritoneal fluid is usually normal (hemorrhagic as necrosis progresses). [Medical therapy (mild, proximal)] Withhold feed for 24-48 hours, IV fluids lactated Ringer's solution 4-6 mL/kg/hr, liquid paraffin 2-4 L via nasogastric tube BID (lubrication/softening), DSS (docusate) 10-20 mg/kg via nasogastric tube (surfactant; particularly effective for tannin-free fiber masses), magnesium sulfate 1 g/kg PO once (osmotic laxative). Warm-water enema (small colon obstruction only). [Pain management] Flunixin meglumine 1.1 mg/kg IV q12h, butorphanol 0.02-0.04 mg/kg IV, butylscopolamine 0.3 mg/kg IV (spasmodic component). [Surgical indications] Laparotomy if refractory to medical therapy for 48 hours, complete obstruction, or signs of ischemia (tachycardia >60, lactate >4). In the small colon, transanal dilation and removal is less invasive than enterotomy. For proximal colon cases, approach via the cecal base/pelvic flexure. [Postoperative] Broad-spectrum antimicrobials (penicillin + gentamicin × 5 days), small amounts of liquid feed after 12-24 hours NPO, transition to normal feed over 1 week. [Recurrence prevention (most important)] Dental examination (correction of sharp crowns), adequate water intake (warmed water in winter), cut forage short (<5cm), avoid feeding poor-quality straw to elderly horses, maintenance psyllium administration (1 week per month).
entries.horse|Copper Poisoning: [Equine Copper Poisoning] Administration of molybdenum and sodium thiosulfate (copper chelation and promotion of excretion via formation of insoluble copper thiomolybdate). Fluid therapy (renal protection + promotion of excretion of haemolysis products). Acute oral ingestion → gastrointestinal decontamination (activated charcoal 1-2 g/kg PO + mineral oil 4-8 mL/kg). If haemolytic anaemia is severe (PCV<15%) → blood transfusion. Hepatoprotection: SAMe 20 mg/kg PO q24h, silymarin. Identify and remove the causative feed (concentrate feeds or mineral blocks with excessive copper content). Horses are more copper-tolerant than ruminants, but large ingestions cause acute haemolytic anaemia and hepatic necrosis. Quantify copper accumulation by liver biopsy.
entries.horse|Cyanide Toxicity: [Cyanide toxicity] Extreme emergency (death can occur within minutes of onset). Antidote: sodium thiosulfate 30-40 mg/kg IV slow. Sodium nitrite 10-20 mg/kg IV slow (alternative agent). Oxygen therapy. Maintain circulation with fluid therapy. Causes: young shoots of sorghum/Johnson grass and after frost damage, wilted cherry leaves. Immediate on-site treatment is essential; there is no time to wait for transport. Keeping the antidote on hand at the farm is recommended. Recovering cases improve within 24 hours.
entries.horse|Equine Glandular Gastric Disease (: [Diagnostic criteria] Examine the pyloric antrum and gastric body in detail by gastroscopy. EGGD is not graded on the ECEIM scale but described (anatomic location, distribution, appearance: hyperemia, linear, erosion, ulceration, fibrin adherence, hemorrhage). The pylorus is difficult to access and lesions are often missed (Sykes et al. JVIM 2015). [First line (ECEIM recommendation)] Omeprazole 4 mg/kg PO SID + sucralfate 12 mg/kg PO BID-TID combined × at least 8 weeks (EGGD takes longer to heal than ESGD). Administration on an empty stomach is preferable. Sucralfate alone has also been reported effective through its mucosal protective action (Hepburn EVJ 2014). [Refractory cases] Misoprostol 5 μg/kg PO BID-TID × 8 weeks (PGE1 analog, promotes mucus and bicarbonate secretion, contraindicated in pregnant mares). Omeprazole + misoprostol in combination may be superior to either alone (Varley et al. EVE 2019). [Injectable omeprazole] Long-acting omeprazole 4 mg/kg IM q5-7 days (marketed in Europe, useful when oral administration is not possible, Sykes et al. EVJ 2017). [Husbandry] 24-hour pasture/forage, stress reduction (one full rest day per week from exercise, stable housing environment), grain restriction. EGGD responds less strongly to dietary management than ESGD, but it remains important as a foundation. [NSAIDs] Discontinue in principle. If continuation is necessary, switch to a COX-2 selective agent (firocoxib 0.1 mg/kg PO SID) + concurrent gastric mucosal protection. [Confirmation of healing] Repeat gastroscopy after 8 weeks; if not healed, an additional 8 weeks. Some cases take 4-6 months to heal completely. [Contracting lesions / outflow obstruction] Long-standing lesions carry a risk of pyloric stenosis; if refractory to medical therapy, consider pyloroplasty. [Maintenance therapy] After healing, sucralfate 12 mg/kg PO SID or BID to prevent recurrence; omeprazole maintenance is decided case by case.
entries.horse|Equine Squamous Gastric Disease (E: [Diagnostic criteria] Gastroscopy (3m flexible endoscope), observing beyond the margo plicatus. ECEIM grade: 0=normal, 1=reddening/hyperkeratosis, 2=small erosions/shallow ulcers, 3=large/multiple ulcers, 4=deep ulcers/hemorrhage (Sykes et al. JVIM 2015). [First choice] Omeprazole 4 mg/kg PO SID × 28 days (GastroGard oral paste, given in the morning after fasting). In mild cases (grade 1-2), 2 mg/kg SID has also been reported to be effective (Sykes & Jokisalo EVJ 2014). [Confirmation of healing] Repeat endoscopy after 4 weeks. If healed, move to maintenance therapy. If not healed, extend by 4 weeks + re-evaluate feeding management. [Maintenance therapy] Omeprazole 1-2 mg/kg PO SID (prevention of rebound ulceration), or discontinue medication if environmental factors can be removed. [Adjunctive therapy] Alfalfa pellets 1-2 kg/day (buffering of gastric acid by calcium, Lybbert et al. J Anim Sci 2007), 24-hour forage access, grain less than 2 g/kg/day. [Feeding before exercise] Feeding 0.5-1 kg alfalfa 30 minutes before exercise prevents gastric acid splash (Nadeau et al. AJVR 2000). [Alternative drug] Ranitidine 6.6 mg/kg PO TID (H2 blocker, when omeprazole is unavailable). Sucralfate alone is ineffective for ESGD. [Prevention of recurrence] Continued feeding management is essential even after healing (recurrence rate >30%, Andrews 2005).
entries.horse|Eyeworm Disease: [Diagnosis] Definitive diagnosis is direct visualization by slit-lamp biomicroscopy of white filiform worms (Thelazia lacrimalis, 1-2 cm long) in the conjunctival sac, beneath the third eyelid, or within the lacrimal duct. After an auriculopalpebral nerve block, evert the conjunctiva under sedation and thoroughly search the posterior surface of the third eyelid and the upper and lower fornices (multiple worms are common). Examine conjunctival sac lavage fluid (physiological saline) microscopically for larvae. As a secondary finding, evaluate secondary corneal ulceration with fluorescein staining. Evaluate concurrent conjunctivitis and dacryocystitis. Take a history of exposure to flies (Musca autumnalis, face fly) during the endemic season (summer to late summer). [Treatment] Mechanical removal: lavage the conjunctival sac with physiological saline and extract the worms with forceps (fine mosquito forceps). Anthelmintics: ivermectin 0.2 mg/kg PO (standard anthelmintic dose), moxidectin 0.4 mg/kg PO, repeat dose after 14 days (both adult and larval stages). Topical neostigmine 0.5% eye drops (Eulimene drops, older therapy); topical antimicrobial (chloramphenicol 1% q6h × 7 days) to prevent secondary bacterial infection; atropine 1% q12h for secondary corneal ulceration. Systemic ivermectin/moxidectin regular deworming program. [Prevention] Fly masks in summer, fly control in stables (permethrin spray, fly traps), manure management on pastures (to suppress fly breeding), regular herd deworming (spring/summer). [Prognosis] >95% good with deworming and mechanical removal; delayed treatment may leave cicatricial conjunctivitis or chronic dacryocystitis; corneal damage is sometimes permanent; reinfection is frequent with inadequate prevention. [References] Lyons et al. J Parasitol 2000; Beelitz et al. Vet Parasitol 1999; Gilger 3rd ed Ch 3; Brooks 2nd ed Ch 3.
entries.horse|Fescue Toxicity: [Fescue toxicity (general)] Removal from endophyte-infected fescue pasture is fundamental. Peripheral vasoconstriction (dry gangrene/laminitis): acepromazine 0.02-0.04 mg/kg IV/IM (vasodilation), keep limbs warm. Agalactia (pregnant mares): domperidone 1.1 mg/kg PO q24h (start 30 days before foaling). Thermoregulatory disturbance (heat intolerance): environmental cooling, water bathing. Conversion to endophyte-free cultivars is the fundamental countermeasure. Move to alternative pasture before foaling.
entries.horse|Fescue Toxicosis: [Endophyte-infected Fescue Toxicosis] Removal from fescue pasture. Reproductive disorders: domperidone 1.1 mg/kg PO q24h (from 30 days before foaling). Peripheral vasoconstriction (limb gangrene/laminitis): acepromazine 0.02-0.04 mg/kg IV/IM. Agalactia → artificial rearing of the foal. Conversion to endophyte-free varieties is the fundamental countermeasure. Novel endophyte MaxQ varieties are also an option.
entries.horse|Fescue Toxicosis (Reproductive): [Dosing basis] *Based on a 500kg mare. [Exposure management (most important; the only definitive treatment)] (1) Move off fescue pasture at ≥270 days of gestation (at the latest by 300 days) (to non-endophyte grasses such as bermudagrass or orchard grass). Plasma prolactin recovers 30-60 days after the move. (2) Complete removal of fescue-contaminated feed (fescue hay and all fescue-containing feeds). [Drug therapy (adjunct when moving is not possible)] (3) Domperidone: D2 antagonist → recovery of prolactin. Dose: 1.1 mg/kg PO SID (550 mg/day for a 500kg horse = 55 mL of 10 mg/mL liquid or 110 x 5 mg tablets), start 30 days before the expected foaling date and continue for 2-3 weeks after foaling. Adverse effects: GI hypermotility (diarrhea). (4) Sulpiride 3.3 mg/kg PO BID (alternative D2 antagonist). (5) Cabergoline (potent D2 antagonist): 0.0014 mg/kg PO q3 days (0.7 mg/dose for a 500kg horse) — reported use in the literature, off-label. [Foaling management and neonatal support] (6) Colostrum supplementation when mammary development is inadequate: donor colostrum 2-4 L within 12 hours (at least 2 L within 6 hours of birth), using commercial colostrum replacer or frozen colostrum. (7) IgG measurement: serum IgG at 18-24 hours of age (target >800 mg/dL; <400 indicates sepsis risk); if low, plasma transfusion (commercial equine plasma 2-4 L IV slow). (8) Keep the neonate warm and provide fluids (address hypoglycemia and dehydration). (9) Management of dystocia: cervical ripening agent PGE2 gel (dinoprostone 0.5 mg intracervical) + oxytocin 5-10 IU IV. (10) Management of retained placenta: oxytocin 10-20 IU IM q4-6h; manual removal only after more than 6 hours have elapsed. (11) Intestinal support (large fetus from prolonged gestation): confirm intestinal motility after colostrum intake, confirm passage of meconium. [References] Redmond et al. Theriogenology 1994; Cross et al. J Anim Sci 1995; Brendemuehl et al. J Anim Sci 1995; Evans et al. Vet Clin Equine 2002.
entries.horse|Foal Gastric Ulcer Syndrome (FGUS): [Clinical classification (Becht)] (1) Silent type: asymptomatic but ulcers on endoscopy; prophylactic treatment. (2) Clinical type: bruxism, ptyalism, dorsal recumbency, inappetence; acid suppression required. (3) Perforating type: acute shock, peritonitis, poor prognosis, emergency laparotomy. (4) Duodenal stricture type: chronic gastric outflow obstruction, surgical management. [Diagnosis] Confirm the margo plicatus region (ESGD) and pyloric antrum (EGGD) with a 1 m small-diameter gastroscope (after 4-6 hours of nursing restriction). In bleeding cases, fecal occult blood is positive; evaluate gastric wall thickening >5 mm and free fluid (perforation) by abdominal ultrasound. [First-line treatment] Omeprazole 4 mg/kg PO SID × 14-28 days (GastroGard, dosed by body weight), given in the morning on an empty stomach (30 minutes before nursing). In severe cases or when oral administration is not possible, pantoprazole 1.5 mg/kg IV SID or ranitidine 6.6 mg/kg IV q6-8h (H2 blocker, practical for ICU foals). [Concurrent mucosal protection] Sucralfate 20 mg/kg PO q6-8h × 14-21 days (2-hour interval from acid suppressants), especially in cases with duodenal involvement. [Symptom control] For colic, butorphanol 0.02-0.04 mg/kg IV; avoid flunixin (NSAIDs worsen the condition). If pain persists, lidocaine CRI 1.3 mg/kg IV bolus → 0.05 mg/kg/min. [Supportive care] IV fluids, lactated Ringer's solution 4-6 mL/kg/hr maintenance; if nursing drive is reduced, milk replacer via nasogastric tube 10-15 mL/kg/hr in small frequent amounts, maintain blood glucose (>80 mg/dL), correct electrolytes. [Treatment of underlying disease] Aggressive treatment of concurrent disease (sepsis, pneumonia, diarrhea, arthritis), broad-spectrum antimicrobials (penicillin 22,000 U/kg IV q6h + amikacin 25 mg/kg IV SID), discontinue NSAIDs or switch to firocoxib. [Surgery for the perforating type] Laparotomy, abdominal lavage, ulcer suture, postoperative antimicrobials and abdominal drain; poor prognosis (survival <30%). [Duodenal stricture type] Diagnosed by chronic gastric distension and vomiting-like reflux; gastroduodenal anastomosis (gastrojejunostomy); long-term postoperative treatment required. [Prevention] Prophylactic omeprazole 2-4 mg/kg PO SID or ranitidine 6.6 mg/kg IV q8h in critically ill foals (NICU, sepsis, surgical) (Furr et al. JVIM 1992), appropriate feeding and stress reduction, avoidance of unnecessary NSAIDs. [Monitoring] Repeat endoscopy after 2-4 weeks to evaluate healing.
entries.horse|Fumonisin Toxicosis (ELEM): [Fumonisin toxicosis (ELEM)] Causes leukoencephalomalacia. No specific treatment. Supportive care: DMSO 1 g/kg IV (reduces cerebral edema), dexamethasone, mannitol. Seizure management. Immediate removal of contaminated feed. Case fatality rate 75-100%. FDA guideline: fumonisin 5 ppm or less in horse feed. Produced in corn by Fusarium verticillioides.
entries.horse|Hepatic Disease: [Diagnosis] Blood chemistry: GGT (most important, biliary), SDH/GLDH (acute hepatocellular injury), AST (nonspecific), total and direct bilirubin, bile acids (>20 μmol/L indicates hepatic dysfunction), ammonia (>60 μmol/L indicates hepatic failure). Coagulation tests (PT/PTT/fibrinogen). Abdominal ultrasound (right 6th-17th intercostal spaces) to assess liver size, echogenicity and biliary dilation. [Liver biopsy (diagnostic gold standard)] Percutaneous 14G biopsy needle (ultrasound-guided, right side, 12th-14th intercostal space) for histologic diagnosis: pyrrolizidine alkaloid toxicosis (megalocytosis), cholangiohepatitis, Theiler's disease, granulomatous hepatitis, etc. Perform after confirming normal coagulation times. [Cause-specific treatment] (1) Chronic active hepatitis/cholangiohepatitis: dexamethasone 0.05-0.1 mg/kg IV/PO SID × 7 days, then taper gradually (assess laminitis risk); antimicrobial (ceftiofur 2.2 mg/kg IV q12h × 7-10 days). (2) Pyrrolizidine alkaloid toxicosis: no specific treatment; stop exposure; supportive care. (3) Hepatic encephalopathy: see dg_hepatic_encephalopathy. [Dietary therapy] Low protein (8-10%), feeds with a high branched-chain amino acid ratio (beet pulp, grain + molasses), methionine and vitamin B complex supplementation; roughage limited to grass hay only (alfalfa contraindicated — high protein load). [Supportive care] Fluids (Ringer's solution with 5% dextrose 2-4 mL/kg/hr, to prevent hypoglycemia), S-adenosylmethionine (SAMe) 20 mg/kg PO SID, ursodeoxycholic acid 10-15 mg/kg PO SID (cholestatic cases), vitamin K1 0.5-1 mg/kg IM q24h × 3 days (coagulopathy). [Poor prognostic indicators] Bile acids >50 μmol/L, prolonged PT, fibrosis >75% on liver biopsy, chronic clinical signs. References: Divers TJ. Liver disease in horses. VCNA Equine Pract 2011;27:1-18; Durham AE. Equine liver disease overview. EVE 2014.
entries.horse|Hepatic Encephalopathy: [Pathophysiology] Central nervous system syndrome due to hepatic insufficiency. In hepatic failure, unprocessed 'toxins' such as ammonia, aromatic amino acids, and GABA-like substances cross the blood-brain barrier → abnormal neurotransmission → altered consciousness and behavioral abnormalities. Develops with blood ammonia >60 μmol/L (normal <35) and loss of >70% of hepatocellular function. Acute form (Theiler's disease, acute intoxication) progresses over days; chronic form is gradual. Mortality 50-80% (depends on underlying liver disease and severity). [Diagnosis] Spectrum of neurological signs: Mild (HE Grade 1-2): behavioral change, depression, fluctuating appetite, mild ataxia. Moderate (Grade 3): head pressing (characteristic), circling, blindness-like behavior, excessive vocalization, unresponsiveness, mild seizures. Severe (Grade 4): coma, seizures, recumbency, decreased pupillary reflexes. Evidence of liver disease: blood chemistry (elevated GGT, AST, SDH, bilirubin >5, bile acids >50, hypoglycemia, hypoalbuminemia, prolonged PT/PTT), blood ammonia >60 μmol/L (strong correlation), abdominal ultrasonography, liver biopsy (after confirming normal coagulation times). Differentiate from other neurological diseases (WNV, EPM, encephalitis, hypoglycemia, EMS, lead poisoning). [Acute treatment (quiet environment essential)] (1) Minimize stimulation: dark, quiet room, head helmet (self-injury from head pressing), prevent hypoglycemia. (2) IV fluids LRS + 5-10% dextrose 2-4 mL/kg/hr (hypoglycemia prevention essential, target blood glucose >80 mg/dL). (3) Reduction of intestinal ammonia (most important treatment): lactulose 0.3 mL/kg PO q6-8h (lowers intestinal pH → ammonia ionization → excretion, promotes osmotic stool), adjust dose if no response (maximum 0.5 mL/kg); conversely, overdose causes diarrhea, dehydration, and electrolyte abnormalities. Neomycin 10-15 mg/kg PO q6h × 3-5 days (suppresses urease-producing bacteria; monitor renal function: nephrotoxicity risk). Metronidazole 15 mg/kg PO q8h (suppresses anaerobes, adjunct for HE improvement, alternative to or combined with neomycin). (4) Branched-chain amino acids (BCAA): intravenous or oral to increase the BCAA/aromatic amino acid ratio; theoretical rationale (clear evidence in horses is limited). (5) Cerebral edema management (severe HE): mannitol 0.25-1 g/kg IV slow × 30 minutes, may repeat, lowers intracranial pressure (recommended by Divers et al. 2011). [Seizure/excitation management] Diazepam 0.02-0.1 mg/kg IV (start at the lowest dose, beware respiratory depression), phenobarbital 5-10 mg/kg IV/PO SID (cautious due to hepatic metabolism), xylazine contraindicated (worsens HE, hypotension). Midazolam 0.02-0.1 mg/kg IV slow (short-acting). [Dietary therapy] Low protein (8-10%), high branched-chain amino acid ratio, grass hay only (alfalfa and high-protein feeds contraindicated), beet pulp + small amounts of grain fed frequently; when oral intake is impossible, nasogastric gruel or PPN (choose amino acids with a higher BCAA ratio than standard). [Treatment of underlying liver disease] See dg_liver_failure. Acute hepatic failure: identify and treat the cause; chronic: immunosuppression (dexamethasone). [Coagulopathy] Vitamin K1 0.5-1 mg/kg IM q24h × 3 days, fresh frozen plasma 2-6 L (active bleeding), bleeding prevention (pressure). [Prognostic indicators] (Durham & Smith-Maxie EVJ 2014) Persistent ammonia >100, rising bilirubin >10, Grade 4 HE, coma, recurrent seizures → poor prognosis. Early treatment of Grade 1-2 gives 30-50% survival; acute Theiler's disease 40-60% possible survival. References: Durham AE. Hepatic encephalopathy in horses. EVE 2005; Divers TJ. VCNA Equine Pract 2011.
entries.horse|Hoary Alyssum Toxicity: [Hoary Alyssum Toxicity] Removal of the causative plant/change of pasture comes first. Fluids (lactated Ringer's IV, correction of dehydration). Limb oedema: reduce with compression bandaging and hydrotherapy. Laminitis prevention: cryotherapy (limb cooling). Phenylbutazone 2.2 mg/kg PO q12h (anti-inflammatory, analgesic). Most recover within 2-4 days after removal of the cause, with a good prognosis. Clinical signs appear when contamination of hay is >30%. Main signs are fever, limb oedema and diarrhoea.
entries.horse|Horse Chestnut Toxicity: [Horse chestnut (Aesculus) toxicity] GI decontamination: activated charcoal 1-2 g/kg PO. Fluid therapy (lactated Ringer's IV). GI protection: sucralfate 20 mg/kg PO q6h. Seasonal myonecrosis type (atypical myopathy, hypoglycin A): fluid therapy (high-volume IV, management of myoglobinuria), vitamin E/selenium, L-carnitine. CK monitoring. Prognosis depends on the extent of myonecrosis.
entries.horse|Internal Parasites: [Diagnosis] Classify horses by fecal egg count (FEC, McMaster or Mini-FLOTAC method): ≥250-500 EPG as high shedders and <200 as low shedders (AAEP Internal Parasite Control Guidelines 2019). If larval cyathostominosis is suspected, evaluate with serum fibrinogen, albumin, and abdominal ultrasound. For tapeworms, serum ELISA antibody or fecal PCR (egg detection sensitivity is low). [Selective deworming (AAEP recommendation)] Deworm only high-shedder horses 2-3 times per year, preserving a low-resistance refugia population. [First-line drugs] Moxidectin 0.4 mg/kg PO (effective against adult and larval strongyles, worms expelled within 24 hours, egg reappearance period 12-16 weeks), or ivermectin 0.2 mg/kg PO (adult strongyles, 8-10 weeks). [Tapeworm control] Praziquantel 1 mg/kg PO (effective against Anoplocephala perfoliata) in combination with ivermectin/moxidectin once or twice a year (autumn). [Larval cyathostominosis] Moxidectin 0.4 mg/kg PO (the only agent effective against mucosally encysted larvae), or fenbendazole 10 mg/kg PO SID × 5 days (power pac). In severe cases, low-dose prednisolone 0.5-1 mg/kg PO SID × 5-7 days, tapering, to suppress the excessive inflammatory response (Peregrine et al. EVJ 2014). [Supportive care] For protein-losing enteropathy, IV fluids and plasma transfusion; for anemia, darbepoetin or similar as appropriate. [Monitoring for anthelmintic resistance] If the fecal egg count reduction test 14 days after deworming is <90%, suspect resistance (Nielsen et al. Vet Parasitol 2022). [Husbandry] Remove feces twice weekly, rotational grazing, avoid overstocking, quarantine and deworm newly arrived horses. References: Reed/Bayly/Sellon Equine Internal Medicine 4th ed 2018, AAEP Parasite Control Guidelines 2019.
entries.horse|Ionophore Toxicosis (Monensin / La: No specific antidote. Supportive care only. Immediate removal of the causative feed. Acute phase: activated charcoal 1-3 g/kg PO (via nasogastric tube — effective within 4 hours of ingestion).  Mineral oil 2-4 L PO (promotes elimination of toxin from the intestinal tract). Heart failure management: fluid therapy (lactated Ringer's), arrhythmia management (lidocaine CRI).  Digoxin 2.2 μg/kg IV q12h → PO (positive inotropy — in chronic heart failure). Vitamin E/Se supplementation: vitamin E 5,000-10,000 IU/day PO (myocardial protection, antioxidant). Rest: strict rest (acute myocardial injury phase — reduces risk of sudden death). Monitoring: echocardiography (once weekly — assessment of myocardial recovery), ECG. Prognosis: acute massive ingestion carries high fatality (50-100%). Subacute cases progress to chronic cardiomyopathy → long-term exercise restriction. Prevention: avoid co-feeding with cattle/poultry feed; prevent contamination at the feed mill.
entries.horse|Lactation Failure: [First-line drug: domperidone] Domperidone 25-30 mg PO BID-TID (dose: 0.5-1 mg/kg). Effect appears in 2-7 days. Taper gradually after confirming a rise in the mare's serum prolactin. [Alternative drug: tramadol] Tramadol 5-6 mg/kg PO TID (normally an analgesic, but μ-receptor stimulation raises prolactin). Used in regions where domperidone is difficult to obtain. Can be combined (synergistic effect). [Metoclopramide] Metoclopramide 0.1-0.2 mg/kg IV q6-8h (weaker effect than domperidone, stronger dopamine blockade). [Nutritional support] Selenium (sodium selenite) 3-5 mg/day IV/IM (from 2-3 days before foaling to after foaling). Vitamin E 2000-3000 IU/day. Copper 80-160 mg/day. Magnesium supplementation (cereal + electrolytes + mineral-balanced feed). [Colostrum replacement] If the foal cannot ingest colostrum, hand-feed a colostrum replacer (Foal-Lac, Equine Gold, etc.). IgG measurement: measure serum IgG at 24-36 hours. If <800 mg/dL, transfuse plasma/serum (administer 250 mL/kg) or commercial dried colostrum (dissolve 60-100 g → nasogastric tube). [Monitoring] Milk composition analysis (milk fat percentage, protein, lactose). Monitor the mare's body weight (prevent overfeeding). Confirm foal growth (weekly body weight).
entries.horse|Lead Poisoning: [Lead poisoning in horses] Chelation therapy: CaEDTA 75 mg/kg IV slow q12h × 5 days, repeat after a 2-day rest. Thiamine 5 mg/kg IV q12h (neuroprotection in lead encephalopathy). Activated charcoal 1-2 g/kg PO + sodium sulfate (insolubilization of lead in the GI tract). Seizures: diazepam 0.05-0.2 mg/kg IV. NSAID: flunixin. Clinical signs at blood lead >0.35 ppm. Prevention: removal of environmental lead such as paint and batteries.
entries.horse|Leukoencephalomalacia (Moldy Corn: No specific treatment — supportive care only. Immediate removal of the causative feed is the top priority. Cerebral oedema management: mannitol 0.5-1.0 g/kg IV (20% solution, administered over 20 minutes).  DMSO 0.5-1.0 g/kg IV (10% solution).  Dexamethasone 0.05-0.2 mg/kg IV q24h (short-term — reduction of cerebral oedema). Seizure management: diazepam 0.05-0.4 mg/kg IV. Hepatoprotection: fluid therapy, branched-chain amino acid preparations, lactulose (management of hepatic encephalopathy). Nursing: safe stall, padded walls, dark environment (reduce stimulation). Prevention: quality control of corn feed (prevent mould growth).  Proper drying at harvest and storage, fumonisin testing. Prognosis: poor. Case fatality rate after onset of neurological signs is 80-100%. Mild cases with early discontinuation can recover.
entries.horse|Mercury Poisoning: [Mercury poisoning] Chelation therapy: dimercaprol (BAL) 3 mg/kg IM q4h x 2 days → q12h x 2 days. D-penicillamine 10 mg/kg PO q12h (chronic cases). Activated charcoal (acute oral ingestion). Fluid therapy (renal protection). Thiamine supplementation. Remove the source (disinfectants, paints, seed treatment agents). Monitor renal function. Prognosis depends on the amount and duration of exposure.
entries.horse|Monensin Poisoning: [Monensin poisoning] Cardiotoxicity. No specific antidote. Activated charcoal 1-3 g/kg (effective only immediately after ingestion). Fluids. Heart failure management: digoxin, furosemide. Vitamin E/selenium (antioxidant). Strict rest (risk of exercise-induced sudden death). Assess myocardial damage by echocardiography. LD50: 2-3 mg/kg (the horse is the most sensitive domestic species). Accidental contamination with cattle feed is common. May progress to chronic heart failure.
entries.horse|Mycotoxicosis: [Mycotoxicosis in horses] Removal of contaminated feed is the top priority. Toxin binders: activated charcoal, clay-based binders (bentonite etc.; added to feed to adsorb residual toxin). Hepatotoxic type (aflatoxin): hepatoprotection (SAMe, silymarin) + liver function monitoring. Nephrotoxic type (ochratoxin): fluids to maintain renal perfusion. Neurotoxic type (fumonisin → leukoencephalomalacia/ELEM): supportive care only, poor prognosis. Prevent by proper drying and storage of feed.
entries.horse|NSAID Toxicity: Immediately discontinue the NSAID. GI protection: omeprazole 4 mg/kg PO once daily (gastric ulcers), sucralfate 20 mg/kg PO every 6-8 hours. Maintain renal perfusion and correct electrolytes with aggressive fluid therapy (lactated Ringer's solution). Plasma infusion for hypoproteinemia. Misoprostol 5 μg/kg PO every 12 hours (right dorsal colitis). Pain management (opioids such as butorphanol — additional NSAIDs are contraindicated). Continuous monitoring of renal function, serum protein and electrolytes.
entries.horse|NSAID Toxicosis (Phenylbutazone /: Discontinuing NSAIDs is the top priority. GI ulceration: omeprazole 4 mg/kg PO q24h, sucralfate 20 mg/kg PO q6-8h. Misoprostol 5 μg/kg PO q8h (mucosal protection — contraindicated in pregnant mares). Right dorsal colitis: metronidazole 15-25 mg/kg PO q12h × 4-6 weeks. Hypoproteinemia: plasma transfusion 6-10 L IV, fluid therapy. Renal injury: high-volume fluids (lactated Ringer's), furosemide 1 mg/kg IV (if oliguric). Pain management: butorphanol 0.01-0.05 mg/kg IV (non-NSAID). Diet: low-fiber, easily digestible feed (beet pulp, pellet mash). Prevention: adherence to NSAID use guidelines — phenylbutazone <4.4 mg/kg/day, minimum effective dose for use beyond 5 days. Reduce dose in ponies. Prognosis: recovery possible with early discontinuation. Guarded prognosis with chronic renal injury or severe colitis.
entries.horse|NSAID-Induced Gastroduodenal Ulcer: [Diagnosis] History of NSAID use (dose and duration) is important. Endoscopy confirms deep ulcers, haemorrhage and fibrin adherence in the glandular region (pyloric antrum), pylorus and proximal duodenum. Hypoproteinaemia and chronic anaemia are frequently concurrent. Positive faecal occult blood suggests gastrointestinal bleeding. Also evaluate concurrent renal impairment (papillary necrosis). [Immediate discontinuation of NSAIDs] Completely discontinue all NSAIDs. Alternative pain management: butorphanol 0.01-0.04 mg/kg IV q4-6h, lidocaine CRI 1.3 mg/kg IV bolus → 0.05 mg/kg/min, gabapentin 5-10 mg/kg PO BID (chronic pain). [Acid suppression (first choice)] Omeprazole 4 mg/kg PO SID × at least 4-6 weeks (healing takes longer in the pyloric and duodenal regions). In severe cases or when oral administration is difficult, pantoprazole 1.5 mg/kg IV SID. [Mucosal protection] Sucralfate 12-20 mg/kg PO q6-8h (on an empty stomach, 2 hours apart from other drugs), misoprostol 2-5 μg/kg PO q8-12h (PGE1 replacement, particularly effective for NSAID injury, contraindicated in pregnant mares). [Cases with duodenal involvement] Concurrent prokinetics (erythromycin 1 mg/kg IV q6h for motilin-like action, or metoclopramide 0.04 mg/kg/hr CRI). [Supportive care] IV fluids lactated Ringer's solution 2-4 mL/kg/hr; plasma transfusion 2-6 L for hypoproteinaemia (albumin <2.0 g/dL); blood transfusion for anaemia with PCV<20%. 24-hour pasture/hay access, small frequent feeds. [Assessment of healing] Repeat endoscopy after 4-6 weeks; extend treatment if not healed. [Future NSAID policy] Complete switch to a COX-2 selective drug (firocoxib 0.1 mg/kg PO SID); permanent discontinuation of phenylbutazone is recommended. Limit to short-term use in the acute phase only. [Monitoring] Evaluate total protein, albumin, PCV and renal function weekly during treatment. [Preventive co-administration] In cases requiring continued NSAIDs, concurrent omeprazole 1-2 mg/kg PO SID; prophylactic sucralfate is also effective (Whitfield-Cargile et al. EVJ 2016).
entries.horse|Nightshade Poisoning: [Nightshade (Solanaceae) poisoning] Remove the causative plants (tomato, potato sprouts/greened parts, eggplant leaves/stems, horse nettle (Solanum carolinense)). GI decontamination: activated charcoal 1-2 g/kg PO. Supportive care: fluid therapy (lactated Ringer's IV), GI protection (sucralfate). Atropine 0.01-0.02 mg/kg IV (for cholinergic signs such as bradycardia). Diarrhea management. Most cases recover with supportive care and the prognosis is good. Solanine/solanidine are the toxic principles. Severe poisoning is rare.
entries.horse|Nitrate Toxicity: [Nitrate toxicity in horses] Methylene blue 1-2% 4-8 mg/kg IV slow (reduces methemoglobin, first line). May be repeated (after 4-6h). Oxygen therapy. Mineral oil 4-8 mL/kg PO (reduces absorption of residual nitrate). Fluids. Chocolate-brown blood is characteristic. Remove the causative feed. Feed nitrate >1% DM is dangerous. Prevention: test forage after drought.
entries.horse|Oleander Toxicity: [Oleander toxicosis] Cardiac glycoside (oleandrin). Decontamination: activated charcoal 1-3 g/kg. Arrhythmia management: atropine 0.005-0.01 mg/kg IV (bradycardia), lidocaine (ventricular tachycardia). Electrolyte management (correction of hyperkalemia). Fluids. Continuous ECG monitoring. A single leaf can reach a lethal dose. Digibind (digitalis antibody) may be effective.
entries.horse|Organophosphate Toxicosis: [Organophosphate toxicosis] Atropine 0.01-0.04 mg/kg IV (repeat until muscarinic signs resolve). Pralidoxime (2-PAM) 20-40 mg/kg IV slow (cholinesterase reactivation; effective within 24 hours of exposure). Decontamination: washing (dermal exposure), activated charcoal (oral exposure). Seizures: diazepam. Respiratory management. ChE activity monitoring.
entries.horse|Persimmon (Phytobezoar) Gastric Im: [Diagnostic keys] History of persimmon fruit ingestion in autumn (persimmon trees in pasture, fallen fruit), persistent large-volume reflux via nasogastric tube, gastroscopic confirmation of a black-green rubbery concretion (phytobezoar). [Trial of medical therapy (mild cases)] Coca-Cola therapy: Coca-Cola classic 2-4 L via nasogastric tube q6-8h × 2-3 days (phosphoric acid and sugar soften persimmon tannin, Kellam et al. EVJ 2000). DSS (docusate) 10-20 mg/kg via nasogastric tube (surfactant softening). Repeated warm-water gastric lavage 2-4 L/session. Withhold feed 48-72 hours + IV fluids lactated Ringer's solution 4-6 mL/kg/hr. [Cases refractory to medical therapy (most cases)] Early laparotomy → direct removal of the phytobezoar by gastrotomy. Rupture risk increases if conservative treatment exceeds 48-72 hours. [Surgical procedure] Gastrotomy (greater curvature side) to remove the phytobezoar, gastric lavage, two-layer closure, peritoneal lavage. Postoperative: antimicrobials (penicillin + gentamicin × 5-7 days), NPO for decompression, stepwise refeeding (liquid feed from 48-72 hours, mash from 1 week, normal feed from 2 weeks), omeprazole 4 mg/kg PO SID × 4 weeks (postoperative gastric mucosal protection). [Pain management] Butorphanol 0.02-0.04 mg/kg IV q4-6h, flunixin 1.1 mg/kg IV q12h (NSAIDs short-term only). [Signs of gastric rupture] Tachycardia >80bpm, congested mucous membranes, signs of peritonitis (hemorrhagic peritoneal fluid, high white cell count), acute deterioration → poor prognosis (mortality >95%). [Prevention is most important] Complete removal of persimmon trees and fallen fruit from pastures in autumn, management of leftover fruit after the persimmon harvest, seasonal monitoring in regions where persimmons are handled.
entries.horse|Phalaris Toxicosis: [Phalaris Toxicosis] Acute form: removal of the causative pasture, supportive care (fluids, rest). Chronic form (Phalaris staggers): difficult to cure (melanin-like pigment deposition in the CNS reflects irreversible neurodegeneration). Cobalt/selenium supplementation (a preventive effect has been reported). Mild cases may improve with removal of the cause. Management of Phalaris aquatica in pastures (adjust timing of cutting). Frequently reported in Australia and elsewhere. The chronic neurological form has a poor prognosis.
entries.horse|Poison Hemlock Toxicity: [Poison hemlock toxicity] Neuromuscular blockade by a nicotinic alkaloid (coniine). Respiratory muscle paralysis is the cause of death. Respiratory support (endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation as needed) is most important. Activated charcoal 1-3 g/kg PO (via nasogastric tube). Atropine 0.01-0.02 mg/kg IV (management of bronchial secretions). Maintain circulation with fluid therapy. For seizures: diazepam. No specific antidote. If respiration can be maintained, recovery is possible within 12-24 hours. Teratogenic risk in pregnant mares.
entries.horse|Pokeweed Toxicity: [Pokeweed (Phytolacca americana) toxicity] Gastrointestinal decontamination: activated charcoal 1-2 g/kg PO (via nasogastric tube). Fluids (lactated Ringer's IV, correction of dehydration). GI protection: sucralfate 20 mg/kg PO. Diarrhea management. For seizures: diazepam 0.05-0.1 mg/kg IV. ECG monitoring (risk of arrhythmias). The roots and berries are the most toxic parts (phytolaccatoxin, phytolaccagenin). Most recover with supportive care and the prognosis is good.
entries.horse|Postpartum Hemorrhage / Uterine Ar: [Initial management — rest and maintaining hypotension are most important] (1) IMMEDIATE QUIET STALL: strict rest, avoid stimulation, darkened stall, family members leave, do not move the mare while standing. Prevent blood pressure elevation to prevent re-bleeding. (2) Transrectal palpation for fluctuation of the broad ligament / palpable hematoma (spherical mass 30-50 cm in diameter, near L4-L5, no systolic fluctuation, sensation of sediment inside) — keep manipulation to a minimum (forceful palpation can rupture the hematoma and induce intra-abdominal hemorrhage). (3) Vitals: monitor HR, RR, mucous membrane color, CRT, tongue color, pulse pressure and temperature q15-30 min. HR>80, CRT>3 seconds, white mucous membranes, reduced pulse pressure and cold extremities indicate severe shock. (4) Ultrasound (transabdominal): free intra-abdominal fluid (hemoperitoneum), size and internal echogenicity of the broad ligament hematoma (tortuous vascular pattern → active bleeding). (5) Abdominocentesis: if peritoneal fluid PCV is >20% of peripheral blood PCV, active intra-abdominal hemorrhage. [Hypotension management (hypotensive resuscitation)] (6) Minimal fluids: isotonic crystalloid (Plasmalyte/LRS) 4-6 L/hr (half the usual dose), target MAP 60-70 mmHg (kept low to prevent re-bleeding). Do not aim for full blood pressure restoration with crystalloids alone (permissive hypotension). (7) Colloids: hetastarch 6% 5-10 mL/kg IV slow drip, or 7.2% saline 4 mL/kg IV bolus; hemoglobin substitute (Oxyglobin 5-15 mL/kg) is effective if available. (8) Transfusion: in cases with PCV<15%, heart rate >80 and rapid progression, whole blood 15-20 mL/kg IV slow drip (cross-matched, Aa/Qa-negative donors preferred) — keep transfusion volume conservative (over-transfusion raises blood pressure → induces re-bleeding). [Promotion of hemostasis] (9) Aminocaproic acid (Amicar) 70 mg/kg IV q6h (fibrin stabilization, antifibrinolytic). (10) Yunnan Baiyao 4-8 g PO q12h (traditional medicine; beware of arrhythmia). (11) Naloxone 0.01-0.02 mg/kg IV slow (improves hypotension, promotes coagulation; controversial). (12) Place cool towels on the abdomen (has a benzodiazepine-like sedative effect; medical evidence limited). [Sedation (prevention of overstimulation)] (13) Acepromazine 0.02-0.04 mg/kg IV slow (α1 antagonism lowers blood pressure → prevents re-bleeding; note contraindication when hypotensive), or butorphanol 0.01-0.04 mg/kg IV q4h; detomidine 0.01-0.02 mg/kg IV slow (α2 agonist, raises blood pressure, so usually avoided). [Surgical intervention] (14) Surgical hemostasis is generally not recommended (re-bleeding and high anesthetic mortality). Only exceptionally, in cases of loss of consciousness, massive intra-abdominal hemorrhage or ruptured hematoma, laparotomy under general anesthesia (survival rate <30%). (15) In cases with intrauterine bleeding only and an intact broad ligament, intrauterine tamponade (gauze packing + sterile saline lavage) may be attempted. [Supportive care] (16) Antimicrobial prophylaxis: ceftiofur 2.2 mg/kg IM/IV BID or cefcapene 22,000 IU/kg IV q6h + gentamicin 6.6 mg/kg IV SID (prevention of infection of the broad ligament hematoma, 3-5 days). (17) Vit K1 0.5-1 mg/kg SC q12h, vitamin C 20 mg/kg IV q12h (vascular wall strengthening, antioxidant). (18) Laminitis prevention: ice baths for 24-72 hours (cooling the DDFT/CL joints), phenylbutazone 2.2 mg/kg IV BID (short-term). (19) Prevention of postpartum uterine disease: oxytocin 10-20 IU IM q6h (promotes uterine involution, low dose); postpone uterine lavage for 24-48 hours because of bleeding risk. [Prognosis] When the broad ligament hematoma does not rupture (contained hematoma), survival rate is 60-80%; if stable for 48-72 hours, long-term prognosis is good. In cases with progressive intra-abdominal hemorrhage, survival rate is 20-30%, and improvement is limited even with aggressive treatment including transfusion. Recurrence risk: 15-25% at the next foaling, and recurrence is especially likely in the same arterial system, so discontinuation of future breeding is recommended in principle. [References] Frazer Equine Vet J 2003; LeBlanc et al. AAEP Proc 2011; Vandeplassche Reproduction in Domestic Animals 1980; McCue et al. JAVMA 2007; Equine Reproduction 2nd ed (McKinnon et al. 2011) Ch.230-232; Robinson/Sprayberry Current Therapy 7th ed Ch.150-151.
entries.horse|Pregnancy Luteal Insufficiency / I: [Dose basis] *Based on a 500 kg mare. All doses are individually adjusted for body weight, BCS and concurrent disease. For administration during pregnancy, always confirm contraindications and teratogenicity. [Progestin supplementation (the foundation of treatment)] (1) Altrenogest (synthetic progestin, altrenogest): trade names Regu-Mate 0.22% (2.2 mg/mL syrup) or Altresyn 4 mg/mL syrup. Standard dose 0.044 mg/kg PO SID = 22 mg/day for a 500kg horse (Regu-Mate 10 mL / Altresyn 5.5 mL, top-dressed on feed or given orally directly by syringe). In recurrent cases, prior EED, or confirmed luteal insufficiency, double dose 0.088 mg/kg PO SID (44 mg/day for a 500kg horse = Regu-Mate 20 mL). Start of administration: (a) with prior history → from D2-5 after ovulation, (b) early loss detected → immediately, (c) placentitis diagnosed → immediately. Duration: at least until D120-140 (waiting for accessory CL regression + establishment of placental progestogen synthesis); in recurrent or refractory cases consider continuing until D250-280 (decide based on the risk from abortion history). Discontinue by tapering over 7-10 days (for a 500kg horse 20 mL→15 mL→10 mL→5 mL→stop); abrupt discontinuation risks inducing abortion. [Handling precautions] Skin contact causes hormonal effects in humans — contraindicated for pregnant women, children and men alike; always wear nitrile gloves and long sleeves; if it contacts skin, wash immediately with soap. (2) Progesterone (natural P4) injection: (a) progesterone in oil 200-500 mg IM SID (standard 300 mg/day for a 500kg horse; sesame oil or corn oil solution 50-100 mg/mL, 3-6 mL IM) — daily IM injections are painful and cause injection-site swelling, making long-term use difficult. (b) BioRelease P4-LA 1.5% (compounded, overseas): 1.5 g IM q7-14 days (for a 500kg horse 100 mL IM per dose, divided between shoulder and gluteal sites) — convenient for long-term pregnancy maintenance. (c) P4 vaginal devices (CIDR, Cue-Mate) have uncertain efficacy in horses and are not first-line. [Selection criteria] Altrenogest is first-line (oral; only the dermal contact risk needs to be managed); injectable P4 for oral intolerance / severe fescue exposure / altrenogest-refractory cases. [Concurrent treatment for placentitis] (3) Antimicrobials: (a) trimethoprim-sulfa (TMS, Tribrissen 480 mg/mL paste or 5 g oral granules) 30 mg/kg PO BID = 15 g/dose BID for a 500kg horse (3 sachets of oral granules) × 2-3 weeks, the standard for placentitis treatment. (b) Severe cases → ceftiofur sodium (Naxcel) 2.2-4.4 mg/kg IM/IV q12h × 3-7 days → ceftiofur crystalline free acid (Excede) 6.6 mg/kg IM, repeat after 4 days (22 mL IM in the neck for a 500kg horse). (c) Procaine penicillin 22,000 IU/kg IM q12h + gentamicin 6.6 mg/kg IV SID × 7-10 days (severe cases, hospitalized). (d) Fungal placentitis: fluconazole 5 mg/kg PO loading → 1-2 mg/kg PO SID × 30-60 days, or itraconazole 5 mg/kg PO SID × 30-60 days. (4) Anti-inflammatory: flunixin meglumine (Banamine 50 mg/mL) 1.1 mg/kg IV/IM q12h = 11 mL for a 500kg horse × 5-7 days; chronic management 0.25 mg/kg PO/IV q8h (low-dose anti-PG, 2.5 mL q8h for a 500kg horse). Watch for GI/renal adverse effects with long-term use. (5) Pentoxifylline (Trental 400 mg tablets) 8.5 mg/kg PO BID = 4,250 mg BID for a 500kg horse (10 tablets BID) × 30 days or longer, TNFα suppression and improved microcirculation. (6) Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) 50-65 mg/kg PO SID = 25-32 g/day for a 500kg horse, improves placental blood flow (continue 4-8 weeks). (7) L-arginine 100 mg/kg PO BID (NO supply → improved uterine blood flow, research level). [Fescue toxicosis] (8) Immediate cessation of exposure: remove endophyte-positive pasture 90 days before foaling (switch to endophyte-free fescue, other grass species or hay). (9) Domperidone (Equidone gel 11% = 110 mg/mL, Prokinet 1%) 1.1 mg/kg PO SID = 5 g/day for a 500kg horse (Equidone 5 mL gel), start 10-15 days before the expected foaling date and continue until at least 5-10 days after foaling (agalactia prevention). In severe cases may increase to 2.2 mg/kg PO BID (10 mL BID). If udder development is inadequate, add hCG 2,500 IU IV on the day of foaling or oxytocin 5-10 IU IM q4h (milking aid). (10) Metoclopramide sulfate 0.2 mg/kg IM q8h is an alternative to domperidone (central adverse effects — watch for extrapyramidal signs). [Concurrent PPID] (11) Pergolide mesylate (Prascend 1 mg tablets) start at 2 μg/kg PO SID = 1 mg/day for a 500kg horse (1 tablet); recheck ACTH after 4 weeks; if inadequate, 2 tablets/day (4 μg/kg). Not teratogenic during pregnancy (FDA: Class B); may be continued. [Infectious disease management] (12) Leptospira: oxytetracycline 6.6-10 mg/kg IV q24h × 5-7 days = 66-100 mL of 50 mg/mL oxytetracycline slow IV for a 500kg horse, as a slow infusion (rapid IV causes collapse), or streptomycin 11 mg/kg IM SID × 5-7 days. (13) EHV-1: acyclovir 10-20 mg/kg PO 5×/day (5,000-10,000 mg/dose for a 500kg horse), limited efficacy (bioavailability <5%). Valacyclovir 27-40 mg/kg PO TID (13.5-20 g/dose TID for a 500kg horse) has higher oral bioavailability. Isolation, group separation, and management of human and horse traffic. [Adjunctive therapy] (14) Fluids (for dehydration or systemic signs): isotonic crystalloids (LRS, Plasmalyte) 2-4 L/hr, target urine output 0.5-1 mL/kg/hr. (15) Vit E (α-tocopherol) 5,000-10,000 IU/day PO (natural d-α recommended; prevention of fetal NMD: combine with Se 3 mg/day). 10,000 IU/day recommended in late pregnancy. (16) Vit C 4-6 g IV/PO SID (antioxidant support). (17) Silymarin (milk thistle) 20-30 mg/kg PO SID (hepatoprotection during long-term antimicrobial use). [Strict rest] (18) Stall rest, minimal pasture turnout (walking only, 1-2 hours per day), complete cessation of transport and training. (19) Stall environment: temperature 18-22°C, fresh air, low dust (dust-free hay / steamed hay). (20) Minimize stress: avoid group separation (keep a companion horse nearby), maintain routine. [Monitoring] (21) Transrectal ultrasound q7-14 days: CL number and vascularity, CTUP (combined thickness of the uterus and placenta cranial to the cervical star — D271-300 <8mm, D331-360 <10mm; values above indicate progressing inflammation), fetal heart rate and activity. (22) Serum progestogens q14 days: (a) D14-100 P4 → target >4 ng/mL, (b) after D100 total progestogens (5α-DHP) → target >4 ng/mL; be alert to a sudden fall (<2 ng/mL) or sudden rise (>10 ng/mL outside the pre-foaling situation). (23) Estrone sulfate (after D60): >1 ng/mL = fetus alive, <0.5 ng/mL suspect fetal death. (24) Maternal CBC, SAA and fibrinogen q14 days (inflammatory markers). [If abortion occurs] (25) Discontinue altrenogest (to prevent a persistent CL after abortion → delayed next estrus). (26) Pathological examination of the placenta and fetus is essential: placental weight (normally 10-11% of foal body weight; >14% suggests placentitis), discoloration and thickened areas on the chorionic surface, culture (aerobic, anaerobic, fungal), PCR (EHV-1/4, EVA, Leptospira), histology. (27) Maternal uterine lavage (warm saline 2-4 L) within 24-48 hours, oxytocin 10-20 IU IM q4-6h × 24 hours, systemic antimicrobials as needed. (28) Rest for at least one cycle (21 days) before the next pregnancy; resting 2-3 cycles is also an option based on recurrence risk assessment. [Prognostic follow-up] For the next pregnancy, after endometrial biopsy + culture + US evaluation, start altrenogest prophylactically with early intervention from D2 after ovulation. [References] McKinnon AO et al. Equine Reproduction 2nd ed (Wiley-Blackwell 2011) Ch.226-235, 250-260 / Allen WR. The diagnosis and treatment of pregnancy failure in the mare. Equine Vet J 2001 / Daels PF et al. Theriogenology 1996 / LeBlanc MM. Theriogenology 2008 / LeBlanc MM. Ascending placentitis in the mare: an update. Reprod Domest Anim 2010 / Macpherson ML. Treatment strategies for placentitis. Theriogenology 2005 / Cross DL. Fescue toxicosis in horses. In Neotyphodium/Grass Interactions 1997 / Stout TAE. Equine reproductive endocrinology. Anim Reprod Sci 2016 / Squires EL et al. Use of altrenogest. Theriogenology 1983 / Plumb's Veterinary Drug Handbook 9th ed / AAEP Theriogenology Committee Guidelines / Robinson NE, Sprayberry KA. Current Therapy in Equine Medicine 7th ed Ch.151-155.
entries.horse|Premature Placental Separation (Re: [Management in the foaling stall — the first 5 minutes are decisive] (1) Immediate incision of the CA membrane: boldly incise the exposed chorioallantois longitudinally with sterile scissors or a scalpel (vulva-to-cervix direction), and expose the amnion and fetus as quickly as possible. Hesitation is fatal — if the membrane is not opened, the fetus will asphyxiate. (2) Assisted delivery: confirm both forelimbs and the head, and apply traction with chains and by hand synchronized with the mare's straining.
